common_name: US-942 Citrandarin (Dwarfing HLB-Tolerant Cold-Hardy Rootstock Hybrid)

planting.note: Graft a desired scion onto young US-942 liners in spring; this dwarfing citrandarin keeps resulting trees notably smaller and is widely planted in Florida replant sites for its tolerance of citrus greening.

directions: US-942 came out of the USDA-ARS citrus breeding program at Fort Pierce, Florida, from a cross of Sunki mandarin and Flying Dragon trifoliate orange, combining two notably cold-hardy parents. It became one of the most widely adopted rootstocks in Florida's post-greening replanting push because it noticeably dwarfs the grafted tree while still producing good yields, a useful trait for home gardeners with limited space. Like other trifoliate-derived understocks, its roots carry far more cold tolerance than the citrus scion grafted onto it, so winter hardiness depends mostly on the variety budded on top. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, and expect a smaller, more manageable tree than on vigorous rootstocks like Carrizo or Volkamer.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm and Rootstock Breeding
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Citrus Rootstock Selection Guide

common_name: US-812 Citrandarin (High-Yield HLB-Tolerant Cold-Hardy Rootstock Hybrid)

planting.note: Graft a desired orange, grapefruit, or mandarin scion onto young US-812 liners in spring; this USDA citrandarin has performed well in Florida trials for yield under greening pressure.

directions: US-812 descends from Sunki mandarin crossed with Benton citrange (itself an older sweet-orange-trifoliate hybrid), giving it a double dose of trifoliate-derived cold hardiness in the root system. In Florida rootstock trials conducted after the spread of citrus greening, it has ranked among the higher-yielding modern selections, making it attractive for growers replacing stock lost to the disease. Trees on US-812 tend toward moderate-to-strong vigor with good fruit quality from the grafted scion, though as with any citrandarin the understock's own small fruit is sour and seedy. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and treat its cold tolerance as a property of the roots, not the scion variety grafted on top.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm and Rootstock Breeding
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Citrus Rootstock Selection Guide

planting.note: Graft a desired citrus scion onto young X-639 liners in spring; this older USDA citrandarin tolerates the heavy, seasonally wet soils common to Gulf Coast flatwoods better than many standard rootstocks.

directions: X-639 is an older USDA citrandarin from a cross of Cleopatra mandarin and trifoliate orange, developed decades before the newer numbered rootstocks bred for greening tolerance. It earned a lasting niche in Florida's flatwoods citrus districts because it handles poorly drained, seasonally waterlogged, high-pH soils better than Swingle citrumelo or the citrange rootstocks, a trait that also suits heavy Gulf Coast clay. The trifoliate parentage gives the roots solid cold tolerance, and trees on X-639 are moderately vigorous with generally good fruit quality from the grafted scion. It has fallen out of mainstream commercial use in favor of newer selections but remains a sound, well-documented choice for a home dooryard tree on imperfectly drained ground.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Citrus Rootstock Selection Guide
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm and Rootstock Breeding

planting.note: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired citrus scion onto the young rootstock; C-35 is grown as an understock, not for its own fruit.

directions: C-35 citrange was selected at the University of California, Riverside from the same sweet-orange-by-trifoliate-orange cross type as Carrizo and Troyer, but specifically chosen for stronger resistance to Phytophthora root rot and citrus nematode. Growers have increasingly turned to it as an alternative where those soil-borne problems limit the older citrange rootstocks, while retaining comparable cold hardiness and good compatibility with most scion varieties. Trees on C-35 tend to be slightly smaller and more precocious than on Carrizo, bearing a bit earlier without a major yield penalty. Plant in full sun on well-drained ground, and graft on a named citrus variety rather than relying on the understock's own bitter, seedy fruit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Citrus Rootstock Selection Guide
